Agent-Diff: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Enterprise API Tasks via Code Execution with State-Diff-Based Evaluation

ISBN: 978-1-4503-XXXX-X/2018/06CCS: Computing methodologiesCCS: Computing methodologies Artificial intelligenceCCS: Computing methodologies Modelling and simulation
Hubert M. Pysklo Affiliation: Minerva University, San Francisco, California, USA email: hubert@uni.minerva.edu , Artem Zhuravel Affiliation: Minerva University, San Francisco, California, USA email: zhuravel@uni.minerva.edu and Patrick D. Watson Affiliation: Minerva University, San Francisco, California, USA email: pwatson@minerva.edu
Received  5 June 2009
Abstract.

We present Agent-Diff, a novel benchmarking framework for evaluating agentic Large Language Models (LLMs) on real-world tasks that execute code via external APIs. Agentic LLM performance varies due to differences in models, external tool access, prompt structures, and agentic frameworks. Benchmarks must make fundamental trade-offs between a sandboxed approach that controls for variation in software environments and more ecologically valid approaches employing real services. Agent-Diff attempts to capture the desirable features of both of these approaches by including access to the real API interfaces for software services while sandboxing the environment in which calls are made, processed, and evaluated. This approach relies on two key innovations. The first is a novel state-diff contract, which separates process from outcome - rather than fuzzy trace or parameter matching, we define task success as whether the expected change in environment state was achieved. The second is a novel sandbox that provides a standardized scripting layer that all models use to execute code against external APIs (Slack, Box, Linear, Google Calendar). Thus, we can evaluate different agentic LLMs against a standardized set of contracts using a unified sandbox while still evaluating their performance on real-world service interfaces. Using the Agent-Diff framework, we provide benchmarks for nine LLMs across 224 tasks utilizing enterprise software workflows. In addition, we evaluate the robustness of the framework with ablation experiments to assess the contribution of access to API documentation on benchmark performance.

Code and data: https://github.com/agent-diff-bench/agent-diff.

Keywords: 
Large Language Models, Evaluation, Agents, Benchmark

1. Introduction

Agentic LLMs  (Yao et al., 2023a) actively interact with external software environments (Masterman et al., 2024) and are capable of code generation and code-centric reasoning (Deng et al., 2025b)  (Anthropic, 2026b) (Google, 2026) (Cursor, 2026). While the dominant paradigm for agent–environment interaction remains tool calling through structured schemas such as the Model Context Protocol (Anthropic, 2024), such approaches face scalability constraints as tool catalogs grow into the hundreds or thousands of definitions (Gao et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). As such, rather than relying on rigid tool definitions, agents can write and execute code to interact with APIs directly (Jones and Kelly, 2025)–an approach that scales more efficiently but demands that agents plan, iterate, and maintain state over extended action sequences. Current benchmarks do not adequately measure these capabilities in enterprise productivity settings–an increasingly common agentic application domain (Anthropic, 2026a).

Existing benchmarks occupy different points in a shared evaluation design space (Li et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2025; Maekawa et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2024). In particular, benchmarks differ along (i) the interaction model (structured tool calling via MCP/JSON schemas (Gao et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025) vs. direct API access (Li et al., 2023) vs. agent-written code (Deng et al., 2025a; Merrill et al., 2026)), (ii) the environment (synthetic or mocked (Gao et al., 2025; Maekawa et al., 2025) vs. live services (Wang et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025) vs. reproducible sandboxes (Yan et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2025a)), (iii) the evaluation signal (trace matching (Gao et al., 2025) vs. outcome/state verification (Yan et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2024) vs. judge-based scoring (Wang et al., 2025)), (iv) the observability assumptions (white-box instrumentation (Yan et al., 2025) vs. black-box APIs (Wang et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025)), and (v) the task horizon. Table 1 summarizes how representative benchmarks align with these axes.

The current work introduces Agent Diff, a benchmarking framework that combines desirable features of both live and sandboxed approaches: agents interact with real API interfaces of enterprise productivity services (Slack, Box, Linear, Google Calendar) inside fully isolated, containerized environments that can be instantiated identically across runs – eliminating the temporal instability inherent in live-service benchmarks. This approach helps maintain ecological validity while maintaining reproducibility and environmental control.

Key to this method is evaluation methodology introduces a state-diff contract that decouples processes and outcome measures. Rather than fuzzy trace or parameter matching, we we compute the state difference between sandbox snapshots at tstartt_{\mathrm{start}} and tendt_{\mathrm{end}} (denoted Δ​S=Diff⁡(Ststart,Stend)\Delta S=\mathrm{Diff}(S_{t_{\mathrm{start}}},S_{t_{\mathrm{end}}})) and define task success by whether the expected change in environment state was achieved. Because diffs are computed over the full environment state, we can enforce invariants and detect unintended side effects (e.g., modifications or deletions of unrelated resources). A standardized scripting layer (supporting both Bash and Python) ensures that all models execute code against external APIs through a unified code-execution sandbox, enabling rigorous comparison across agents.

We use these state-diff contracts to evaluate models across a novel benchmark suite comprising 224 tasks. These tasks include single- and multi-step actions that orchestrate workflows across scheduling, messaging, file management, and project management.

2. Related Work

A core trade-off in agent evaluation is between ecological fidelity and reproducibility. Benchmarks that evaluate agents against mocked or synthetic tool environments (Li et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2025; Maekawa et al., 2025) gain determinism but can underspecify real enterprise API behavior (Bandlamudi et al., 2025). Benchmarks that connect to live services (Wang et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025) increase realism but introduce temporal instability, requiring dynamic ground-truth retrieval. Bandlamudi et al. (Bandlamudi et al., 2025) bridge this gap by comparing agent API responses against ground-truth executions, but their response diffing validates only return values and not whether the intended state change was achieved or whether an unrelated state was inadvertently modified.

Many evaluation protocols validate how an agent acted rather than what it accomplished. Trace-based scoring (Gao et al., 2025; Maekawa et al., 2025) – matching an expected tool-call sequence – is brittle to equivalent alternative strategies and does not guarantee that the intended state change occurred. τ\tau-Bench (Yao et al., 2024) advances evaluation by comparing database state against annotated goals in simulated retail and airline domains, but checks only the target state – not whether unrelated state was inadvertently modified. Reliance on LLM-as-a-judge (Wang et al., 2025) introduces further risk: such judges can be non-deterministic and biased toward stylistic features rather than correctness (Luo et al., 2025). Approaches that instrument application internals (Yan et al., 2025) improve observability but presume open-source or modifiable systems, misaligned with closed-source enterprise SaaS constraints.

A separate line of work evaluates agents that write and execute code rather than invoke structured tool calls. SWE-Bench (Deng et al., 2025a) and Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al., 2026) test code-executing agents in containerized environments, but target software engineering and system administration tasks respectively, with white-box evaluation (unit tests, filesystem inspection). Neither addresses black-box enterprise API interaction, where the agent cannot inspect service internals and must rely solely on API responses to verify its actions.

Agent Diff addresses these limitations simultaneously. Our containerized replicas of production APIs provide ecological fidelity with full reproducibility – without the temporal instability of live services or the oversimplification of mocked environments. Deterministic state diffing evaluates what changed rather than how, capturing both intended outcomes and unintended side effects – unlike goal-state comparison, response diffing, or trace matching. And by targeting code-executing agents against black-box enterprise APIs, we fill the gap left by code-execution benchmarks that assume white-box access.

3. Agent-Diff

Agent-Diff evaluates code-execution agents on long-horizon enter- prise API tasks and evaluates how state changed in the environment. The framework requires: (i) black-box equivalence – closed-source APIs can be faithfully replicated from their public contracts; (ii) state-centric modeling – all operations reduce to typed, state transitions that can be diffed; and (iii) deterministic isolation – each run starts from an identical snapshot.

3.1. Agent-Diff Environments

Our central design hypothesis is that closed-source enterprise APIs can be replicated with sufficient fidelity to produce representative evaluation scores because the contract – not the implementation – defines correctness from an agent’s perspective.

Consider an API as a function f:(ℛ,S)→(S′,𝒪)f:(\mathcal{R},S)\rightarrow(S^{\prime},\mathcal{O}) mapping requests and state to new state and outputs. An agent observes only ℛ\mathcal{R} and 𝒪\mathcal{O}; the internal path from SS to S′S^{\prime} is opaque.

Two implementations ff and f^\hat{f} are behaviorally equivalent over ℛ∗\mathcal{R}^{*} if:

(1) ∀r∈ℛ∗,S:f⁡(r,S)=f^​(r,S)\forall\,r\in\mathcal{R}^{*},\,S:\;f(r,S)=\hat{f}(r,S)

Full equivalence over all possible requests is neither achievable nor necessary. We target equivalence over the subset ℛ∗⊂ℛ\mathcal{R}^{*}\subset\mathcal{R} exercised by the benchmark tasks. Because the APIs in our benchmark are predominantly CRUD interfaces over typed entities, internal side effects (notifications, analytics, caching) are invisible to the agent and irrelevant for evaluation – our replicas need only produce equivalent outputs for equivalent inputs.

Crucially, all information required to construct f^\hat{f} is publicly available: entity schemas (via OpenAPI or GraphQL introspection), operation semantics, response formats (via official SDKs), and error conditions (Slack Technologies, 2026b; Box, Inc., 2026a; Google LLC, 2026; Linear Inc., 2026b). We validate replica fidelity through automated conformance testing against production APIs and adversarial edge-case probing (Appendix 8.10).

State-Centric Modelling.

We model each service as a state machine where state SS is a typed relational database. Entity types (User, Channel, Message in Slack; File, Folder in Box, etc.) map to tables with schemas derived from public API specifications. All operations reduce to three transitions:

(2) Insert :S→S∪{e}\displaystyle:S\rightarrow S\cup\{e\}
(3) Update :S→(S∖{e})∪{e′}\displaystyle:S\rightarrow(S\setminus\{e\})\cup\{e^{\prime}\}
(4) Delete :S→S∖{e}\displaystyle:S\rightarrow S\setminus\{e\}

Rather than validating API call traces, we snapshot all tables before and after agent execution and compute the state difference:

(5) Δadd\displaystyle\Delta_{\text{add}} =Tafter∖Tbefore\displaystyle=T_{\text{after}}\setminus T_{\text{before}}
(6) Δdel\displaystyle\Delta_{\text{del}} =Tbefore∖Tafter\displaystyle=T_{\text{before}}\setminus T_{\text{after}}
(7) Δmod\displaystyle\Delta_{\text{mod}} ={(e,e′):e.pk=e′.pk∧e≠e′}\displaystyle=\{(e,e^{\prime}):e.\text{pk}=e^{\prime}.\text{pk}\land e\neq e^{\prime}\}

The resulting DiffResult – containing all inserted, deleted, and modified entities – is compared against the task’s expected state changes.

Deterministic Isolation.

Each benchmark run instantiates a fresh, isolated environment. We leverage PostgreSQL’s schema isolation: each environment operates within its own schema namespace (e.g., state_{env_id}), enabling concurrent execution without cross-contamination. Environments are seeded from deterministic templates, ensuring identical initial states S0S_{0} across runs. This architecture guarantees that for any task τ\tau and agent 𝒜\mathcal{A}:

(8) ∀r1,r2∈Runs​(τ,𝒜):S0(r1)=S0(r2)\forall r_{1},r_{2}\in\text{Runs}(\tau,\mathcal{A}):S_{0}^{(r_{1})}=S_{0}^{(r_{2})}

enabling reproducible evaluation without the temporal instability of live APIs. To support state diffing, we snapshot all entity tables immediately before and after agent execution, creating immutable copies TbeforeT_{\text{before}} and TafterT_{\text{after}} within the same isolated schema. Because each environment is fully independent, snapshots are free from interference by concurrent runs, and the resulting diffs reflect only the actions of the evaluated agent. Figure 1 illustrates the sandbox architecutre and end-to-end request flow.

3.2. Agent-Diff Benchmark

Task taxonomy.

Each task τ\tau is characterized along five dimensions (Table 3), which arise at different stages of the construction pipeline.

The primary axis is the task horizon n∗​(τ)n^{*}(\tau): the minimum number of endpoint invocations required under an optimal policy, directly controlled via the sampling procedure described below.

Two structural dimensions emerge from the sampled endpoint multiset:

  • •

    Operation profile: the set of API primitives required – search, create, read, update, and/or delete (non-exclusive).

  • •

    Entity scope dscoped_{\mathrm{scope}}: single-entity vs. multi-entity state changes.

Two pragmatic dimensions are shaped during generation and human curation:

  • •

    Information availability dinfod_{\mathrm{info}}: whether required identifiers are provided explicitly in the prompt or must be discovered via API queries. This is governed by the identifier policy in the generation prompt.

  • •

    Ambiguity dambd_{\mathrm{amb}}: the degree to which the prompt underspecifies the exact target. Low-ambiguity tasks are produced by the LLM; medium- and high-ambiguity variants are introduced during human curation (e.g., removing explicit identifiers, adding distractor entities).

These dimensions operationalize problem space beyond trace-level tool calling: agents must search for missing identifiers, plan multi-step workflows, and maintain state across dependent operations.

Tool-call budget.

We target a heavy-tailed distribution of task horizons by sampling intended tool-call counts from a shifted truncated exponential over {1,…,40}\{1,\ldots,40\} with rate λ=0.3\lambda=0.3:

(9) Pr[n=k]∝e−λ⁡(k−1),k∈{1,…,40}.\Pr[n=k]\propto e^{-\lambda(k-1)},\quad k\in\{1,\ldots,40\}.

This yields a target mean of 𝔼⁡[n]≈4.3\mathbb{E}[n]\approx 4.3, biased toward short tasks with a controlled tail of long-horizon scenarios. After feasibility filtering and manual curation, the realized distribution has mean n¯∗=5.3\bar{n}^{*}=5.3 with range 1–24, reflecting a slight upward shift from the rejection of trivially simple proposals.

Endpoint sampling.

For each service ss (Slack, Box, Linear, Google Calendar), let ℰs\mathcal{E}_{s} denote the supported endpoints. Conditioned on ss and the target horizon nn, we sample an intended endpoint multiset (e1,…,en)(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n}) i.i.d. from

(10) Pr[ei=e]=1|ℰs|,e∈ℰs.\Pr[e_{i}=e]=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{E}_{s}|},\ \ \ e\in\mathcal{E}_{s}.

Uniform sampling encourages coverage across the full API surface. The benchmark spans 108 unique endpoints (Box: 27, Slack: 25, Linear: 19, Calendar: 37), with each task requiring a mean of 4.3 distinct endpoints (range 1–12).

Task generation pipeline.

For each sampled endpoint multiset, we use a mix of frontier LLMs (Claude Opus 4 and Gemini 3 Pro) to generate: (1) a natural-language user prompt whose completion induces state changes consistent with (e1,…,en)(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n}), (2) a deterministic seed template defining the initial sandbox state S0S_{0}, and (3) a set of declarative assertions describing the expected state diff and forbidden side effects. The endpoint multiset determines the structural dimensions of the task: its operation profile and entity scope. The generation prompt additionally controls information availability (dinfod_{\mathrm{info}}) by instructing the model whether to expose identifiers explicitly or require the agent to discover them via API queries. In some cases, we supply a pre-authored seed template and ask the model to generate only the prompt and assertions; in others, the model constructs all three components jointly. The full generation prompt is provided in Appendix 8.9.

Human curation.

Each generated task is validated for executability in the sandbox –infeasible samples are discarded or regenerated. Reviewers verify that required identifiers are discoverable and that the necessary endpoints and permissions exist under the stated prompt constraints. Reviewers then control the ambiguity dimension (dambd_{\mathrm{amb}}) by selectively degrading prompts: removing explicit identifiers, introducing typographical variations, or adding distractor entities to the seed state. All tasks are annotated along the five taxonomy dimensions post-hoc to verify broad coverage (Table 3).

Benchmark summary.

The resulting benchmark comprises 224 tasks across four enterprise services: Box (file management), Linear (project management), Slack (messaging), and Google Calendar (scheduling). Table 3 summarizes the distribution across taxonomy dimensions. Three design choices are worth noting: (1) implicit information dominates (66% of tasks), forcing agents to discover identifiers via API queries rather than receiving them in the prompt; (2) multi-entity tasks (53%) require coordinated state changes across multiple tables; and (3) each service exercises distinct API semantics – Box emphasizes nested hierarchies and permissions, Slack stresses threading and multi-party DMs, Calendar demands temporal reasoning and free/busy queries, and Linear involves issue dependencies and workflow state machines.

4. Evaluation Methodology

State-diff evaluation.

Each task τ\tau executes in an isolated sandbox with initial state S0S_{0} and final state S1S_{1}. We compute a canonical state diff Δ​S​(τ)=Diff⁡(S0,S1)\Delta S(\tau)=\mathrm{Diff}(S_{0},S_{1}), consisting of inserted, deleted, and updated entities across all tables (Section 8.8). Scoring depends only on Δ​S​(τ)\Delta S(\tau), not on the agent’s action trace.

Declarative verification logic.

To avoid brittle operation matching, we express task requirements as a set of predicates evaluated on Δ​S​(τ)\Delta S(\tau). Each assertion specifies: (i) a diff_type (added/deleted/updated), (ii) an entity (table), (iii) a conjunction of field-level constraints in where (e.g., equality, substring), and (iv) an expected_count. This forms a compact, implementation-agnostic verification layer that can be authored without writing imperative database queries.

Figure 2 shows the assertions for a two-step Box task (“Delete the misfiled copy, then tag the correct one”). The first assertion checks that the misfiled file was removed (deleted); the second verifies that the tag was applied (updated). Because this task has |A⁡(τ)|=2|A(\tau)|=2 assertions, it contributes weight 2 to the aggregate score – a task with 10 assertions would contribute weight 10, ensuring that complex multi-step tasks are not underrepresented.

Closed-world invariant.

Let A⁡(τ)A(\tau) denote the set of required assertions for task τ\tau and F⁡(τ)F(\tau) the set of fields explicitly marked as ignored. Each task’s assertion set and ignore-list has been manually reviewed to exclude non-deterministic third-order effects (e.g., updated_at timestamps) while capturing all semantically meaningful state changes. We enforce a closed-world invariant: every entity change in Δ​S​(τ)\Delta S(\tau) must be accounted for by some assertion in A⁡(τ)A(\tau) or involve only fields in F⁡(τ)F(\tau). Any unaccounted diff – an unexpected insertion, deletion, or field mutation – is treated as a side effect and the task score is set to zero. Formally,

(11) clean(τ)=𝟙[ΔS(τ)∖cover(A(τ),F(τ))=∅],\mathrm{clean}(\tau)=\mathbb{1}\big[\Delta S(\tau)\setminus\mathrm{cover}(A(\tau),F(\tau))=\emptyset\big],

where cover\mathrm{cover} denotes the set of diffs explained by assertions or ignored fields. This prevents an agent from achieving a high score by completing the requested actions while simultaneously corrupting unrelated state.

Scoring metrics.

Let sat⁡(a,Δ​S)∈{0,1}\mathrm{sat}(a,\Delta S)\in\{0,1\} indicate whether assertion aa holds on the state diff. We define three metrics:

Pass rate. A binary indicator of full task completion with no side effects:

(12) Pass(τ)=clean(τ)⋅𝟙[⋀a∈A⁡(τ)sat(a,ΔS)=1].\mathrm{Pass}(\tau)=\mathrm{clean}(\tau)\cdot\mathbb{1}\Big[\bigwedge_{a\in A(\tau)}\mathrm{sat}(a,\Delta S)=1\Big].

Score. An assertion-weighted measure that gives proportionally more credit to complex tasks. Each task contributes s⁡(τ)=clean⁡(τ)⋅∑a∈A⁡(τ)sat⁡(a,Δ​S)s(\tau)=\mathrm{clean}(\tau)\cdot\sum_{a\in A(\tau)}\mathrm{sat}(a,\Delta S) out of a maximum m⁡(τ)=|A⁡(τ)|m(\tau)=|A(\tau)|. The aggregate score across a task set 𝒯\mathcal{T} is

(13) Score⁡(𝒯)=∑τ∈𝒯s⁡(τ)∑τ∈𝒯m⁡(τ),\mathrm{Score}(\mathcal{T})=\frac{\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}s(\tau)}{\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}m(\tau)},

so a 10-assertion task that passes 8 assertions but triggers an unexpected deletion contributes (0,10)(0,10), not (8,10)(8,10). This weighting ensures that long-horizon tasks with many verification points are not underrepresented relative to simple single-assertion tasks.

5. Experiments

5.1. Experiment Setup

Prompting & Interaction.

We utilize the ReAct prompting framework (Yao et al., 2023b) adapted for code execution. The system prompt 8.6 instructs the model to reason about the task and emit a code block (Bash) to interact with the environment.

Documentation conditions.

To disentangle reasoning ability from prior API knowledge, we evaluate each model under three conditions. No-docs (∼400{\sim}400 tokens): the prompt contains only the service name, base URL, and ReAct instructions; the agent must discover endpoints by probing the API. Relevant-docs (∼3,200{\sim}3{,}200–10,00010{,}000 tokens): the target service’s API specification is injected into the prompt (Table 10). All-docs (∼22,300{\sim}22{,}300 tokens): specifications for all four services, testing whether irrelevant documentation degrades performance via context dilution. No-docs serves as the primary baseline (Table 4); documentation effects are measured relative to it (Table 5).

Sandbox Execution Environment.

Model responses are parsed to extract Bash code blocks, which are executed in a stateless containerized environment. The sandbox is equipped with standard Linux utilities (jq, curl, grep, sed) and a stateless (test-to-test) local filesystem for intermediate file manipulation. Crucially, all network traffic is intercepted and routed to our local service replicas (Slack, Linear, Box, Google Calendar). To the agent, these replicas are indistinguishable from real upstream APIs in terms of latency, headers, and error schemas.

Inference Parameters.

We evaluate the models listed in Table 11 (Appendix) via the OpenRouter API using each provider’s default temperature. Each model uses its full context window; episodes that exceed the context or token limit are marked as failed. An episode terminates when the agent emits a <done> token, the trace reaches 40 turns, or wall-clock time exceeds 8 minutes.

Evaluation Protocol.

Every test case instantiates a fresh sandbox with a deterministically seeded database state. We perform 3 trials per (task, documentation-condition) combination across 3 conditions (no-docs, relevant-docs, all-docs), yielding 9 runs per task per model and 2,016 traces per model (224 tasks ×\times 9). We log full conversation traces, token usage, cost, and number of tool invocations for efficiency analysis.

Bayesian bootstrap aggregation.

We quantify uncertainty via the Bayesian bootstrap (Rubin, 1981) with a uniform Dirichlet prior, placing no a priori preference among tasks. For a set of nn tasks, we draw task weights 𝐰∼Dirichlet⁡(𝟏n)\mathbf{w}\sim\mathrm{Dirichlet}(\mathbf{1}_{n}) and compute the assertion-weighted score

(14) S^(b)=∑iwi(b)​si∑iwi(b)​mi,\hat{S}^{(b)}=\frac{\sum_{i}w_{i}^{(b)}\,s_{i}}{\sum_{i}w_{i}^{(b)}\,m_{i}},

where sis_{i} is the mean raw score for task ii (averaged over trials) and mi=|A⁡(τi)|m_{i}=|A(\tau_{i})| is the maximum possible score. We repeat for B=10,000B=10{,}000 draws, reporting the posterior mean and 95% credible interval (CrI) from the empirical distribution of {S^(b)}b=1B\{\hat{S}^{(b)}\}_{b=1}^{B}. The Dirichlet⁡(𝟏n)\mathrm{Dirichlet}(\mathbf{1}_{n}) prior is the standard non-informative choice, treating all tasks as equally likely before reweighting.

For the documentation ablation, we compare three conditions: no_docs (baseline), relevant_docs (target service only), and all_docs (all four services). We use a paired Bayesian bootstrap: the same Dirichlet draw 𝐰(b)\mathbf{w}^{(b)} is applied to both conditions over their shared task set, yielding a posterior over Δ(b)=S^A(b)−S^B(b)\Delta^{(b)}=\hat{S}_{A}^{(b)}-\hat{S}_{B}^{(b)} with correctly correlated credible intervals on the treatment effect. We report Pr[Δ>0]\Pr[\Delta>0] as the posterior probability that documentation improves performance. Cells with Pr[Δ>0]>0.9\Pr[\Delta>0]>0.9 indicate confident beneficial effects; Pr[Δ>0]<0.1\Pr[\Delta>0]<0.1 indicates confident harmful effects.

6. Experiment Results

6.1. Model-to-model comparison

Table 4 reports per-service and overall assertion-weighted scores under the no-docs baseline, where agents receive no API documentation and must discover endpoints through exploration.

Overall ranking.

DeepSeek-v3.2 leads with an overall score of 88.1 (95% CrI: ±\pm2.4), followed closely by Devstral-2512 at 86.0. These two models form a clear top tier, separated from the next cluster (Qwen3-VL through Gemini-3-Flash, 73.8–79.2) by a gap of ∼7{\sim}7 points. The bottom tier – Claude-Haiku-4.5 (49.3) and Llama-4-Scout (38.0) – scores below 50%.

Service-level variation.

No single service is universally easiest or hardest. Linear yields the highest scores for most models (grand mean 71.4), likely because its issue-tracking API follows predictable CRUD conventions. Calendar proves challenging for models that otherwise perform well: Gemini-3-Flash scores 80.3 on Box but only 62.2 on Calendar, suggesting that temporal reasoning and free/busy queries pose distinct difficulties.

Cost efficiency.

Grok-4.1-Fast achieves the best cost efficiency at $0.01/test (Score/$ = 7,489), outperforming models 5–8×\times more expensive. Claude-Haiku-4.5 is both the most expensive ($0.22/test) and among the worst performers, yielding only 224 Score/$ – a 33×\times gap relative to Grok. Token consumption varies modestly (128k–199k), suggesting that cost differences are driven primarily by per-token pricing rather than verbosity.

6.2. Documentation effects

Table 5 reports the effect of injecting API documentation into the system prompt, measured as the score delta relative to the no-docs baseline with paired Bayesian bootstrap posterior probabilities.

Documentation improves pass rates but not partial-credit scores.

Documentation produces a significant overall increase in pass rate under relevant-docs (Δ=+7.0±2.3\Delta=+7.0{\tiny\pm 2.3} pp, P=1.00P=1.00), with 6 of 9 models showing individually significant improvements (P>0.975P>0.975). The effect is strongest for Box (+14.0+14.0 pp), Calendar (+8.4+8.4 pp), and Linear (+6.3+6.3 pp), all with P=1.00P=1.00, but absent for Slack (+0.5+0.5 pp, P=0.61P=0.61). However, the assertion-weighted score shows a smaller, non-significant aggregate improvement (Δ¯=+2.4\bar{\Delta}=+2.4, P=0.73P=0.73). This divergence suggests that documentation helps agents complete simpler tasks outright (improving pass rate) while providing diminishing returns on complex multi-assertion tasks (diluting the weighted score). Per-model effects remain heterogeneous: the same condition that helps one model on a given service may hurt another (e.g., relevant-docs on Calendar: Qwen3-VL ++12.3, P=1.00P=1.00 vs. Claude-Haiku −-11.9, P=0.02P=0.02).

All-docs: inconclusive overall, harmful on Linear.

Aggregated across services, all-docs yields no reliable score gain (Δ¯=+0.2\bar{\Delta}=+0.2, P=0.53P=0.53) despite still improving pass rates (+6.8+6.8 pp, P=1.00P=1.00). The harm is concentrated on Linear (Δ¯=−4.0\bar{\Delta}=-4.0), where five models show confident or suggestive degradation (e.g., GPT-OSS-120B: −-14.9, P=0.01P=0.01; Kimi-K2: −-13.4, P<0.01P<0.01). Relevant-docs for the same service is near-neutral (++1.7), indicating that the degradation may stem from irrelevant documentation competing for attention in the context window.

Box and training-data familiarity.

Box is the only service with a suggestive aggregate score benefit from documentation (relevant: Δ¯=+10.0\bar{\Delta}=+10.0, P=0.92P=0.92; all-docs: ++7.6, P=0.81P=0.81). In July 2025, Box introduced a Hub API (Box, Inc., 2025) – a new set of endpoints for organizing content into shared hubs. Because these endpoints post-date the training cutoffs of most evaluated models, they provide a natural experiment: Hub tasks test the agent’s ability to use genuinely novel APIs, while standard file/folder tasks exercise APIs well represented in pre-training corpora.

Documentation effect is concentrated in Hub tasks.

Table 6 splits Box tasks into Hub (n=13n=13) and Non-Hub (n=35n=35) subsets. Under relevant-docs, Hub tasks improve by Δhub=+19.0±10.5\Delta_{\mathrm{hub}}=+19.0{\tiny\pm 10.5} (P=1.00P=1.00), compared to Δnon​-​hub=+3.4±4.4\Delta_{\mathrm{non\text{-}hub}}=+3.4{\tiny\pm 4.4} (P=0.93P=0.93). A paired test yields P⁡(Δhub>Δnon​-​hub)=0.999P(\Delta_{\mathrm{hub}}>\Delta_{\mathrm{non\text{-}hub}})=0.999, providing strong evidence that the documentation benefit is disproportionately concentrated in Hub tasks. The pattern holds under all-docs (Δhub=+19.6\Delta_{\mathrm{hub}}=+19.6 vs. Δnon​-​hub=+4.8\Delta_{\mathrm{non\text{-}hub}}=+4.8; P⁡(Δhub>Δnon​-​hub)=1.00P(\Delta_{\mathrm{hub}}>\Delta_{\mathrm{non\text{-}hub}})=1.00).

Training-data familiarity hypothesis.

The top-tier models show the starkest contrast: DeepSeek-v3.2 and Devstral-2512 each gain ∼+31{\sim}+31 points on Hub tasks (P=1.00P=1.00) but are essentially flat on Non-Hub tasks (Δ=−1.0\Delta=-1.0, −1.9-1.9; P⁡(Δ>0)<0.4P(\Delta>0)<0.4), indicating that the Box documentation benefit in Table 5 is disproportionately driven by Hub endpoints. The asymmetry is consistent with a training-data explanation: models already encode standard Box file and folder endpoints from pre-training, so documentation adds little for Non-Hub tasks (P=0.93P=0.93). Hub endpoints, introduced after most training cutoffs, are genuinely novel –without documentation, models must discover them through trial and error, yielding substantially lower baseline scores (Hub: 54.1 vs. Non-Hub: 73.1). This asymmetry highlights a methodological concern: tasks built on well-known APIs risk measuring memorization rather than generalizable tool-use ability. Including recently introduced or synthetic endpoints – as the Hub subset naturally provides – offers a more rigorous test of inference-time documentation learning.

6.3. Failure and Recovery Modes

Error taxonomy and annotation.

We annotate 4,032 traces (9 models ×\times 224 tasks ×\times 2 documentation conditions) using an LLM judge (Gemini 3 Flash) with a structured schema covering 32 fine-grained error types (Appendix 9.1). For reporting, these are merged into five error causes – Endpoint Selection, Parameter Errors, Execution Errors, Hallucination, and Reasoning Failures – plus one failure mode (Incomplete Execution). Categories are non-exclusive; definitions and examples are in Appendix 9.3.1.

Error prevalence and recoverability.

Figure 4 plots each error category by prevalence (x-axis) and recovery rate (y-axis) under both documentation conditions. Three patterns emerge. First, documentation uniformly shifts categories leftward (lower prevalence), with the largest reductions for Reasoning Failures (−25.9-25.9 pp) and Hallucination (−21.2-21.2 pp). Second, recovery rates improve across all error causes when documentation is available, with Parameter Errors gaining +21.3+21.3 pp and Reasoning Failures +20.8+20.8 pp. Third, Incomplete Execution remains anchored in the low-recovery zone regardless of documentation (0.00.0% in both conditions), indicating that agents which fail to attempt sub-tasks rarely recover even with better information.

Endpoint Selection is rare under relevant-docs (0.50.5%) but nearly always fatal: no run with this error passed in either condition. In contrast, Execution Errors are moderately prevalent (2323–3030%) but the most recoverable category, reaching 54.854.8% recovery with documentation – suggesting that agents can parse error messages and retry successfully when the endpoint choice is correct.

Relevant documentation reduces API knowledge errors.

We define API knowledge errors as endpoint selection mistakes plus parameter misuse. Under relevant-docs, both absolute and proportional measures decline. The absolute rate (errors per test) decreases for all 9 models, while the proportion of errors attributable to API knowledge gaps decreases for 8 of 9. This dual decline – fewer raw errors and a smaller share of the error budget – indicates that documentation remedies API knowledge deficits more than all errors in general (Appendix 8.2).

Recovery strategies and model tiers.

The most common recovery strategies are break_into_steps (86.8% of runs) and lookup_correct_value (79.8%); the least common are wait_and_retry (0.3%), use_fallback (7.4%), and switch_tool (7.6%). Bayesian bootstrap (Rubin, 1981) with task-level clustering reveals that lookup_correct_value (8/9 models significant) and break_into_steps (6/9) are the strongest positive predictors of task score, while retry_same (8/9) and use_fallback (7/9) predict failure. Comparing top-tier models (DeepSeek, Devstral, Qwen, Kimi) against bottom-tier via median split (Figure 5), top models employ verify_prerequisites and break_into_steps at significantly higher rates (P=1.00P=1.00), while bottom models rely on retry_same (P<0.01P<0.01). Excluding Llama-4-Scout as a statistical outlier (Appendix 8.5), change_strategy and lookup_correct_value also distinguish top performers (P=1.00P=1.00), while backtrack and retry_modified_params lose significance – suggesting these were driven primarily by Llama-4-Scout’s behavior. Overall, higher-performing models favor adaptive, information-seeking recovery over repetitive strategies (Appendix 8.3).

7. Conclusion

We introduced Agent-Diff, a benchmark for code-executing LLM agents on enterprise API tasks. Containerized replicas of production APIs provide ecological fidelity with full reproducibility, and a state-diff evaluation contract enables reproducible, declarative assertions that verify expected state changes while enforcing a closed-world invariant to detect unintended side effects. Evaluating nine models across 224 tasks, we find scores ranging from 38.0 to 88.1, with documentation effects that are service- and model-specific: pass rates improve significantly (+7.0+7.0 pp, P=1.00P=1.00) while assertion-weighted scores do not (+2.4+2.4, P=0.73P=0.73). A training-cutoff natural experiment validates our inclusion of recently introduced endpoints, which isolate inference-time learning from pre-training memorization. Error and recovery analysis reveals that top-performing models favor adaptive strategies (lookup, decomposition) over repetitive ones (retry-same), indicating that planning quality differentiates model tiers beyond API knowledge alone. Code and infrastructure is released under MIT at https://github.com/agent-diff-bench/agent-diff.

8. Appendix

8.1. Error Prevalence Analysis

We analyze error prevalence – the frequency with which different error types manifest across model runs. This complements the recovery strategy analysis by characterizing what goes wrong rather than how agents respond. Understanding error patterns helps identify systematic weaknesses in agent capabilities.

8.1.1. Error Category Taxonomy

Through qualitative coding of agent trajectories, we identified errors across three high-level domains (tool use, hallucination, and reasoning), which we consolidated into 6 merged categories for interpretability: endpoint selection, parameter errors, execution errors, reasoning failures, and incomplete execution. Each error category is coded as binary (present/absent) per run, allowing a run to exhibit multiple error types simultaneously. More information on each of those categories is presented in Appendix 9.1.

8.1.2. Prevalence Rate Analysis

Table 7 reports the percentage of runs in which each error category was observed, stratified by model. This analysis covers all n=3,955n=3{,}955 analyzed runs.

Computation.

For each model mm and error category ee, we compute:

Prevalencem,e=|{r∈Rm:e∈r}||Rm|×100\text{Prevalence}_{m,e}=\frac{|\{r\in R_{m}:e\in r\}|}{|R_{m}|}\times 100

where RmR_{m} denotes the set of runs for model mm, and e∈re\in r indicates that error category ee was coded as present in run rr.

Category Merging.

The 6 merged categories consolidate 35 fine-grained error annotations as follows:

  • •

    endpoint_selection ←\leftarrow tool_use_errors.endpoint_selection

  • •

    parameter_errors ←\leftarrow tool_use_errors.parameter_misuse ∨\lor hallucination_errors.parameter_hallucination

  • •

    execution_errors ←\leftarrow tool_use_errors.format_errors ∨\lor tool_use_errors.code_errors

  • •

    hallucination ←\leftarrow ⋁\bigvee {outcome, state, action, context, capability, other}_hallucination

  • •

    reasoning_failures ←\leftarrow ⋁\bigvee {16 reasoning error subtypes, excluding incomplete/premature}

  • •

    incomplete_execution ←\leftarrow reasoning_errors.incomplete_execution_error ∨\lor reasoning_errors.premature_termination_error

Interpretation.

The heatmap reveals that reasoning_failures (53.6% overall) and parameter_errors (43.3%) are the most prevalent error categories, suggesting that logical reasoning and correct parameterization remain challenging for current agents. Hallucination affects over one-third of runs (36.8%), indicating persistent grounding issues.

endpoint_selection errors are relatively rare (10.3%), suggesting that models generally identify the correct API operations even when they struggle with parameter details or execution.

Notably, llama-4-scout exhibits substantially elevated error rates across all categories – particularly reasoning_failures (86.5% vs. 53.6% overall) and parameter_errors (80.9% vs. 43.3% overall). This model also shows the highest endpoint_selection error rate (35.0% vs. 10.3% overall), a 3.4×\times elevation that is unique among evaluated models.

In contrast, deepseek-v3.2 demonstrates the lowest error rates across most categories, with particularly low hallucination (12.3%) and incomplete_execution (8.0%) rates, consistent with its position as a top-performing model.

8.2. Bayesian Bootstrap Analysis of API Knowledge Errors

To rigorously assess whether documentation reduces API knowledge errors, we employ a clustere Bayesian bootstrap (Rubin, 1981) approach that accounts for test-level dependencies and provides full posterior uncertainty quantification.

Error definition.

We define API knowledge errors as the sum of two error categories extracted from our qualitative coding of agent trajectories:

  • •

    Endpoint selection errors: Calls to non-existent endpoints, use of deprecated APIs, or selection of inappropriate endpoints for the task.

  • •

    Parameter misuse: Incorrect argument types, missing required fields, malformed values, or violation of parameter constraints.

These categories capture failures attributable to incomplete or incorrect knowledge of the API specification, as distinct from logical errors, execution failures, or environmental issues.

Experimental design.

For each model, we compare runs under two conditions: no_docs (no API documentation provided) and with_docs (relevant API documentation included in context). We compute the delta as Δ=statistic​(no_docs)−statistic​(with_docs)\Delta=\text{statistic}(\texttt{no\_docs})-\text{statistic}(\texttt{with\_docs}), such that positive values indicate documentation reduces errors.

Clustering by test.

Because the same test may appear under both documentation conditions, observations are not independent. We cluster by test_id to ensure that bootstrap resampling respects this paired structure. Specifically, we restrict analysis to tests that appear in both conditions (shared tests only), then apply Dirichlet-weighted resampling at the cluster level rather than the observation level. This approach is analogous to a paired bootstrap but accommodates for potentail unequal numbers of runs per test.

Bootstrap procedure.

We use Bayesian bootstrap (Rubin, 1981) with
Dirichlet(1,1,…,1)(1,1,\ldots,1) reweighting (Rubin, 1981). For each of n=100,000n=100{,}000 draws:

  1. (1)

    Sample Dirichlet weights 𝐰∼Dir​(𝟏)\mathbf{w}\sim\text{Dir}(\mathbf{1}) for each group independently, with dimension equal to the number of observations in that group.

  2. (2)

    Compute the weighted statistic for each group.

  3. (3)

    Record the delta (group A statistic minus group B statistic).

From the resulting posterior distribution of deltas, we extract:

  • •

    Posterior mean Δ¯\bar{\Delta}

  • •

    95% credible interval [Δ2.5,Δ97.5][\Delta_{2.5},\Delta_{97.5}]

  • •

    Posterior probability P⁡(Δ>0)P(\Delta>0) and P⁡(Δ<0)P(\Delta<0)

We consider effects significant when P⁡(Δ>0)>0.95P(\Delta>0)>0.95 or P⁡(Δ<0)>0.95P(\Delta<0)>0.95. All analyses use a fixed random seed (42) for reproducibility.

Two complementary metrics.

We report two distinct statistics to guard against interpretive artifacts:

  1. (1)

    Ratio (Figure 6): API knowledge errors as a proportion of total errors, computed as

    ratio=∑iwi⋅api_errorsi∑iwi⋅total_errorsi\text{ratio}=\frac{\sum_{i}w_{i}\cdot\text{api\_errors}_{i}}{\sum_{i}w_{i}\cdot\text{total\_errors}_{i}}

    This metric answers: What fraction of errors are API-knowledge-related?

  2. (2)

    Absolute rate (Figure 7): API knowledge errors per test, computed as the weighted mean

    rate=∑iwi⋅api_errorsi\text{rate}=\sum_{i}w_{i}\cdot\text{api\_errors}_{i}

    This metric answers: How many API knowledge errors occur per test?

The distinction matters because a reduction in the ratio could arise from either (a) fewer API knowledge errors, or (b) more non-API errors inflating the denominator. By reporting both metrics, we can distinguish these scenarios:

  • •

    If ratio decreases but absolute rate is unchanged: documentation increases other error types, not a genuine improvement.

  • •

    If absolute rate decreases but ratio is unchanged: documentation reduces all error types proportionally.

  • •

    If both decrease: documentation targets API knowledge gaps more than non-API knowledge gaps.

Reproducibility.

The bootstrap analysis uses a fixed random seed (42) for reproducibility. Results, along with metadata including model lists and bootstrap parameters, are saved to JSON.

8.3. Recovery Strategies Analysis

We analyze recovery strategies – the behavioral patterns agents exhibit when encountering errors or obstacles during task execution. This analysis proceeds in two stages: first, we characterize the frequency with which different strategies are employed across models (usage rates); second, we evaluate whether employing each strategy is associated with better or worse task outcomes (scores).

8.3.1. Recovery Strategy Taxonomy

Through qualitative coding of agent trajectories, we identified 13 distinct recovery strategies (plus an “other” category), descriptions of which are available in Appendix 9.2. Each strategy is coded as binary (present/absent) per run, allowing a run to exhibit multiple strategies.

8.3.2. Usage Rate Analysis

Table 8 reports the percentage of runs in which each recovery strategy was observed, stratified by model. We restrict this analysis to the n=3,625n=3{,}625 runs where at least one recovery strategy was identified (i.e., excluding runs with no observable recovery behavior; note, that no change of recovery strategy when needed is expected to be handled by the retry_same case). The percentage was calculated following the same procedure as the prevalence of errors in Appendix 8.1 but now applied to recovery strategies.

Interpretation.

The heatmap reveals substantial cross-model consistency in strategy preferences: break_into_steps (86.8% overall) and lookup_correct_value (79.8%) dominate across all models, suggesting these are near-universal recovery behaviors for capable agents. Conversely, retry_same (12.1%) and wait_and_retry (0.3%) are rarely employed, indicating that modern agents generally avoid naive retry loops.

Notable model-specific deviations include Llama-4-Scout, which exhibits elevated usage of retry_same (40.8% vs. 12.1% overall) and parse_error_message (73.8% vs. 46.3% overall), suggesting a qualitatively different error-handling style.

8.4. Per-Model Strategy Effectiveness

Usage rates alone do not establish whether a strategy helps or harms task performance. A frequently-used strategy might be popular precisely because it is ineffective (agents keep trying it) or because it is effective (agents learn to rely on it). To disentangle usage from impact, we estimate the association between of each strateand on task scores using Bayesian bootstrap.

Estimand.

For each model mm and strategy ss, we estimate:

Δm,s=𝔼[Score∣s=1,m]−𝔼[Score∣s=0,m]\Delta_{m,s}=\mathbb{E}[\text{Score}\mid s=1,m]-\mathbb{E}[\text{Score}\mid s=0,m]

where s=1s=1 indicates the strategy was used in a run and s=0s=0 indicates it was not. A positive Δ\Delta implies that runs employing the strategy score higher on average; a negative Δ\Delta implies they score lower.

Bayesian bootstrap methodology.

We employ the Bayesian bootstrap (Rubin, 1981) to quantify uncertainty in our estimates via posterior resampling weights. For each bootstrap iteration b∈{1,…,B}b\in\{1,\ldots,B\} where B=10,000B=10{,}000:

  1. (1)

    Draw Dirichlet weights: Sample 𝐰(b)∼Dirichlet​(𝟏n)\mathbf{w}^{(b)}\sim\text{Dirichlet}(\mathbf{1}_{n}) independently for each group, where nn is the number of observations in that group. This is equivalent to placing a uniform prior over the probability simplex.

  2. (2)

    Compute weighted statistics: For each group (strategy-used vs. strategy-not-used), compute the weighted mean score:

    S¯(b)used=∑i:si=1wi(b)⋅Scorei\bar{S}^{(b)}_{\text{used}}=\sum_{i:s_{i}=1}w_{i}^{(b)}\cdot\text{Score}_{i}

    and similarly for S¯not-used(b)\bar{S}^{(b)}_{\text{not-used}}.

  3. (3)

    Record delta: Store Δ(b)=S¯used(b)−S¯not-used(b)\Delta^{(b)}=\bar{S}^{(b)}_{\text{used}}-\bar{S}^{(b)}_{\text{not-used}}.

From the BB bootstrap samples, we extract:

  • •

    Posterior mean: Δ¯=1B​∑bΔ(b)\bar{\Delta}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b}\Delta^{(b)}

  • •

    95% credible interval: [Δ2.5%,Δ97.5%][\Delta_{2.5\%},\Delta_{97.5\%}] (percentiles)

  • •

    Posterior probability: P(Δ>0)=1B∑b𝟏[Δ(b)>0]P(\Delta>0)=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b}\mathbf{1}[\Delta^{(b)}>0]

Clustering by test.

A critical design decision is whether to account for the nested structure of our data: multiple runs may share the same underlying test (task), inducing correlation in the scores. We cluster by test_id to ensure that bootstrap resampling respects this structure.

Specifically, rather than resampling individual runs, we resample at the cluster (test) level. This approach:

  • •

    Preserves the paired/matched structure when comparing conditions

  • •

    Produces appropriately wider confidence intervals that reflect true uncertainty

  • •

    Avoids overstating precision due to pseudo-replication

Minimum usage threshold.

We exclude strategies with fewer than 5% usage in a given model to avoid unstable estimates from extremely sparse cells. This threshold balances statistical reliability against comprehensiveness.

Significance criteria.

We consider an effect confidently beneficial if P⁡(Δ>0)≥0.95P(\Delta>0)\geq 0.95, suggestively beneficial if 0.90≤P⁡(Δ>0)<0.950.90\leq P(\Delta>0)<0.95, and symmetrically for harmful effects using P⁡(Δ<0)P(\Delta<0). These thresholds correspond to conventional 90% and 95% credible intervals excluding zero.

Reproducibility.

All bootstrap analyses use a fixed random seed (42) for reproducibility. Results are persisted to JSON with full metadata including model lists, strategy sets, thresholds, and bootstrap parameters.

8.4.1. Interpreting Effectiveness Results

Table 9 presents the per-model effectiveness rankings. Several patterns emerge:

Universally beneficial strategies.

lookup_correct_value and
break_into_steps rank in the top 2–3 positions for nearly all models, with consistently positive deltas (Δ=+6\Delta=+6 to +31+31 points) and high confidence (P>0.95P>0.95 or P>0.90P>0.90). These strategies likely succeed because they address fundamental sources of API errors: incorrect parameter values and task complexity.

Universally harmful strategies.

retry_same appears in the bottom 1–2 positions for all models, with strongly negative deltas (Δ=−10\Delta=-10 to −36-36 points, P>0.95P>0.95). This confirms intuition: repeating failed actions without modification is counterproductive. Notably, the magnitude of harm is larger for higher-performing models, possibly because these models encounter retry_same situations only when genuinely stuck.

Model-dependent strategies.

parse_error_message shows heterogeneous effects: beneficial for gpt-oss (Δ=+3.8\Delta=+3.8) but harmful for deepseek-v3 (Δ=−5.5\Delta=-5.5, P=0.98P=0.98) and grok-4.1 (Δ=−9.1\Delta=-9.1, P=0.99P=0.99). This may reflect differences in how models utilize error information – some may overfit to misleading error messages while others extract actionable guidance.

Causal interpretation caveats.

While we frame Δ\Delta as an effect, the observational nature of our data precludes strong causal claims. The association between strategy use and outcomes may be confounded by:

  • •

    Task difficulty: Harder tasks may elicit both more recovery attempts and lower scores.

  • •

    Agent capability: More capable agents may both employ sophisticated strategies and achieve higher scores independently.

  • •

    Error type: Certain error types may trigger specific strategies while also being intrinsically harder to recover from.

We mitigate these concerns through within-model comparisons (controlling for capability) and test-level clustering (partially controlling for task difficulty), but residual confounding remains possible. The effectiveness estimates should be interpreted as associations conditional on model and test, not as guaranteed performance improvements from strategy adoption.

8.5. Median Split Analysis: Recovery Strategy Usage by Model Performance

To investigate whether high-performing and low-performing models differ systematically in their recovery strategy usage, we conducted a median split analysis comparing strategy adoption rates between performance tiers.

8.5.1. Model Performance Ranking and Group Assignment

Models were ranked by their overall benchmark performance scores and divided into two groups at the median. This yielded the following assignment:

  • •

    Top 4 Models (High Performers): DeepSeek-V3, Devstral-Small, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, Kimi-K2-Instruct

  • •

    Bottom Models (Low Performers): Grok-3-Mini-Beta, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Preview, GPT-4.1-Mini, Claude-3.5-Haiku, Llama-4-Scout (excluded in sensitivity analysis)

The median split approach was chosen over arbitrary thresholds because it creates balanced comparison groups and is robust to the specific performance values observed. By comparing the top half against the bottom half, we maximize statistical power while maintaining interpretable group definitions.

8.5.2. Llama Exclusion Rationale

We conducted two parallel analyses: one including all 9 models (Top 4 vs Bottom 5) and one excluding Llama-4-Scout (Top 4 vs Bottom 4). We conducted a test excluding Llama as a sensitivity analysis, since Llama would be classified as a statistical outlier using the Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) method. The modified Z-score for each model was computed as:

(15) Mi=0.6745×(xi−x~)MADM_{i}=\frac{0.6745\times(x_{i}-\tilde{x})}{\text{MAD}}

where x~\tilde{x} is the median score (74.9) and MAD is the median absolute deviation (6.4). This procedure assumes that the model scores {xi}\{x_{i}\} are measured on a common scale and are comparable across models. We treat the median x~\tilde{x} as a robust estimate of the central tendency and MAD=median⁡(|xi−x~|)\mathrm{MAD}=\mathrm{median}(|x_{i}-\tilde{x}|) as a robust estimate of dispersion, which is appropriate when a small number of scores may be extreme. The constant 0.67450.6745 is included to put the statistic on an approximate standard normal “zz-score” scale under a normal reference model: if Z∼𝒩⁡(0,1)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), then median⁡(|Z|)=0.6745\mathrm{median}(|Z|)=0.6745, implying σ≈MAD/0.6745\sigma\approx\mathrm{MAD}/0.6745 for normal data. Using the standard threshold of |M|>3.5|M|>3.5, Llama-4-Scout (M=−3.89M=-3.89) was identified as a statistical outlier.

Llama’s classification as a statistical outlier may indicate a meaningfully different recovery-strategy profile that both (1) places it at a comparative disadvantage under our evaluation setup and (2) exerts disproportionate influence on summary statistics and group-level comparisons.

The primary analysis includes Llama, with the exclusive analysis reported for transparency.

8.5.3. Strategy Filtering

To ensure reliable estimates, we excluded recovery strategies with very low usage rates. Specifically, a strategy was included in the analysis only if it met a minimum 5% usage threshold in at least one of the two groups. This filtering serves three purposes:

  1. (1)

    Noise reduction: Strategies used in only a handful of runs produce highly variable bootstrap estimates.

  2. (2)

    Actionable focus: Very rare strategies are less relevant for understanding systematic behavioral differences.

  3. (3)

    Statistical validity: Bootstrap resampling becomes unreliable when the base rate approaches zero.

Excluded strategies (typically use_fallback, wait_and_retry, handle_ui_obstacle) were documented but not analyzed.

8.5.4. Bayesian Bootstrap Procedure

For each recovery strategy passing the usage threshold, we computed the difference in usage rates between the top and bottom groups using Bayesian bootstrap (Rubin, 1981) with test-level clustering.

Statistic of Interest.

For each strategy ss, we compute:

(16) Δs=p^stop−p^sbottom\Delta_{s}=\hat{p}_{s}^{\text{top}}-\hat{p}_{s}^{\text{bottom}}

where p^sgroup\hat{p}_{s}^{\text{group}} is the weighted proportion of runs in that group that employed strategy ss. A positive Δ\Delta indicates higher usage among top-performing models; a negative Δ\Delta indicates higher usage among bottom-performing models.

Bootstrap Resampling.

We used a paired clustered Bayesian bootstrap designed for comparing two groups that share the same experimental units. The procedure operates as follows:

  1. (1)

    Cluster definition: Runs were clustered by a composite key combining test_id and include_api_docs, treating each (test case ×\times documentation condition) pair as a separate experimental unit.

  2. (2)

    Paired weighting: For each bootstrap draw, we generated a single set of Dirichlet(1,1,…,1)(1,1,\ldots,1) weights over the shared clusters. Critically, the same cluster weight was applied to both the top-performing and bottom-performing model groups. This ensures that when comparing strategy usage rates, both groups are evaluated on identically-weighted tasks.

  3. (3)

    Within-group size correction: Within each group, observations sharing a cluster divided that cluster’s weight equally. If cluster cc received Dirichlet weight wcw_{c} and contained nA(c)n_{A}^{(c)} observations in group A, each observation received weight wc/nA(c)w_{c}/n_{A}^{(c)}. This ensures each cluster contributes equally to the group statistic regardless of how many models completed that task.

  4. (4)

    Statistic computation: For each draw, we computed the weighted usage rate in each group and took their difference: Δ=p^top−p^bottom\Delta=\hat{p}_{\text{top}}-\hat{p}_{\text{bottom}}.

Formally, the procedure computes:

(17) Δ=∑cwc⋅(X¯A(c)−X¯B(c))\Delta=\sum_{c}w_{c}\cdot\left(\bar{X}_{A}^{(c)}-\bar{X}_{B}^{(c)}\right)

where wc∼Dirichlet​(1,…,1)w_{c}\sim\text{Dirichlet}(1,\ldots,1), and X¯A(c)\bar{X}_{A}^{(c)} is the mean strategy usage within cluster cc for group A.

This paired design controls for task-level confounds: if a particular test case is unusually difficult or easy, that effect cancels out when computing the within-cluster difference. The approach is analogous to a paired tt-test but with Bayesian uncertainty quantification and proper handling of multiple observations per cluster.

We used 10,000 bootstrap draws with random seed 42 for reproducibility. Posterior summaries include the mean, 95% credible interval (2.5th–97.5th percentiles), and directional probabilities P⁡(Δ>0)P(\Delta>0) and P⁡(Δ<0)P(\Delta<0).

Inference.

From the 10,000 bootstrap draws of Δs\Delta_{s}, we computed:

  • •

    Posterior mean: 𝔼⁡[Δs]\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{s}]

  • •

    95% credible interval: [2.5th percentile,97.5th percentile][\text{2.5th percentile},\text{97.5th percentile}]

  • •

    Directional probabilities: P⁡(Δs>0)P(\Delta_{s}>0) and P⁡(Δs<0)P(\Delta_{s}<0)

Results were classified according to the following scheme:

  • •

    Significantly higher in top models: P⁡(Δ>0)>0.95P(\Delta>0)>0.95

  • •

    Significantly lower in top models: P⁡(Δ<0)>0.95P(\Delta<0)>0.95

  • •

    Not significant: Neither probability exceeds 0.95

The 0.95 threshold was chosen as the Bayesian analogue to a two-sided α=0.10\alpha=0.10 frequentist test, providing a balance between sensitivity and specificity appropriate for exploratory analysis.

8.5.5. Interpretation and Relationship to Effectiveness Analysis

The median split analysis addresses a fundamentally different question than the per-model effectiveness analysis presented in Appendix 8.4. While effectiveness asks “does using strategy ss improve scores within a model?”, the median split asks “do better-performing models use strategy ss more frequently?”

These questions are complementary and can yield different answers:

  • •

    A strategy might be effective but equally adopted: universally beneficial strategies that all models have learned to employ at similar rates.

  • •

    A strategy might be more common in top models but not causally beneficial: the correlation may reflect model sophistication or training differences rather than the strategy itself driving performance.

  • •

    A strategy might be both differentially adopted and effective: potential drivers of performance differences, where top models have learned behaviors that genuinely improve outcomes.

8.5.6. Sensitivity Analysis: Effect of Llama Exclusion

Excluding Llama-4-Scout from the bottom group reveals several shifts in the comparative analysis, as represented in Figure 8.

Effect of Llama-4-Scout Exclusion.

Robust findings. Three strategies – verify_prerequisites, break_into_steps, and lookup_correct_value – remain significantly more common among top-performing models regardless of Llama’s inclusion. These represent proactive, forward-looking behaviors: verifying preconditions before acting, decomposing problems into manageable steps, and retrieving authoritative information. Similarly, retry_same remains significantly less common among top performers in both analyses, indicating that simply repeating failed actions without modification is a reliably poor strategy.

Llama-driven effects. The parse_error_message strategy was excluded from the analysis when Llama was removed, indicating that it fell below the 5% usage threshold in one or both groups. This suggests Llama disproportionately relied on parsing error messages – a reactive strategy that responds to failures rather than preventing them.

Masked effects. Two strategies – change_strategy and skip_and_continue – emerged as significantly more common among top performers only after Llama was excluded. This pattern suggests that Llama’s usage of these strategies obscured a genuine difference between performance tiers.

Attenuated effects. The strategies retry_modified_params and backtrack shifted from significantly underrepresented among top performers to non-significant when Llama was excluded. This indicates that Llama’s behavior amplified the apparent gap.

Implications.

These results reveal that Llama-4-Scout is not merely a low-scoring model but exhibits qualitatively distinct recovery behavior. Specifically:

  1. (1)

    Reactive over proactive: Llama’s reliance on parse_error_message and elevated use of retry-based strategies (retry_modified_params, backtrack) suggest a reactive error-handling pattern – responding to failures after they occur rather than anticipating and preventing them.

  2. (2)

    Outlier masks structure: Llama’s extreme behavior obscured two meaningful differences (change_strategy, skip_and_continue) that distinguish top from bottom performers among the remaining eight models.

  3. (3)

    Core differentiators are robust: The three most predictive strategies of high performance – verify_prerequisites, break_into_steps, and lookup_correct_value – are unaffected by Llama’s inclusion.

  4. (4)

    Retry without modification is universally poor: The retry_same strategy remains the only robustly underrepresented behavior among top performers, suggesting that the ability to recognize when repetition is futile is a consistent marker of effective agents.
